name: Minoxidil extended-release (VDPHL01)

card.summary: An experimental once-daily extended-release oral minoxidil tablet in late-stage development to regrow and thicken thinning scalp hair.
card.note: Investigational; not an approved product. Oral minoxidil can cause blood-pressure, fluid-retention and excess-hair effects.

quick.overview:
VDPHL01 is an extended-release oral form of minoxidil developed by Veradermics for hair loss. Oral minoxidil in low doses has been used off-label for hair regrowth, and an extended-release version aims to improve efficacy, tolerability, or both for people who do not want or cannot manage topical minoxidil.
As of September 2025 it was in phase 3 trials. Trial results have not been published, so its performance is not yet established.
quick.how: As an investigational drug it is available only through clinical trials. Oral minoxidil in general is a prescription medicine taken by mouth, with hair benefits reported to appear over about 2 to 4 months and peak near 12 months, and hair loss returning after stopping.
quick.risks: Oral minoxidil is associated with low blood pressure, fluid and salt retention, swelling, fast heartbeat, dizziness, headaches and excess hair growth. Rare serious effects include fluid around the heart or lungs. It is contraindicated in some conditions and in pregnancy, and decisions belong with a physician.

lead: VDPHL01 is an investigational extended-release oral minoxidil formulation developed by Veradermics to treat hair loss. Minoxidil was developed by Upjohn in the 1960s and approved as an oral blood-pressure drug in 1979, after which hair growth was noticed as a side effect. Topical minoxidil was approved for male hair loss in 1988 and sold over the counter from 1996.[1]

The appeal for appearance is a denser head of hair. Low-dose oral minoxidil has been used off-label since around 2015 as an option for people who struggle with topical products, and interest rose sharply after an August 2022 New York Times article.[1] An extended-release tablet is being developed to aim for improved efficacy or tolerability. As of September 2025 VDPHL01 was in phase 3 trials, and results were not reported on the source page consulted.[1]

chain: Minoxidil acts on hair follicles and prolongs growth
angle.text: The drug is being developed so that people with thinning hair could take a tablet instead of applying a topical solution. Reported oral minoxidil benefits appear after about 2 to 4 months and peak near 12 months.

sections.h: Background: oral minoxidil for hair loss
paras: Oral minoxidil is used mainly at low doses and off-label for hair loss, while topical forms are the approved route. It is considered effective and well tolerated for people who have trouble with topical use, since long-term adherence to topical minoxidil is low. Results take 2 to 4 months to appear, peak around 12 months, and hair loss returns after stopping.[1]

Extended-release oral minoxidil is being developed with the aim of improving efficacy, tolerability or both. VDPHL01 is the candidate from Veradermics. A separate low-dose sublingual formulation from Samson Clinical was also in phase 3 as of September 2025.[1]

Oral minoxidil side effects include low blood pressure, fluid and salt retention, swelling, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, headaches and excess hair growth. Rare serious effects include pericardial effusion, pleural effusion, cardiac tamponade and pseudoacromegaly, which are reported as much less common at low doses. It is contraindicated in conditions such as pheochromocytoma and pericarditis and in pregnancy.[1]
No results have been published for VDPHL01 itself; phase 3 trials were under way as of September 2025.[1]

timeline.event: Oral minoxidil approved as a blood-pressure drug.[1]
Topical minoxidil approved for male hair loss.[1]
August New York Times article accompanies a surge of interest in low-dose oral minoxidil.[1]
